blocking_rules.description: deduping route 1: surname sound plus both parts of the date of birth. The workhorse — it measured 19.2M pairs over 5.16M representatives there, which is the route the pair budget is really sized for.
blocking_rules.sql: l.surname_metaphone = r.surname_metaphone AND l.dob_year_clean = r.dob_year_clean AND l.dob_month_clean = r.dob_month_clean

blocking_rules.description: deduping route 2: first three letters of the surname, the forename initial and the date of birth. Catches a surname the metaphone splits.
blocking_rules.sql: substr(l.surname_clean, 1, 3) = substr(r.surname_clean, 1, 3) AND l.forename_initial = r.forename_initial AND l.dob_year_clean = r.dob_year_clean AND l.dob_month_clean = r.dob_month_clean

blocking_rules.description: deduping route 3: the middle-name-robust fingerprint — the sorted letters of forename and surname. Catches a filing that carries a middle name against one that does not.
deduping route 4, the typo rescue: same postcode district and same surname sound, where a mistyped date of birth would have hidden the pair from route 1.

deduping route 5, the marriage route: the forename sound and the date of birth agree while the surname sound does not. Route 1 already has the same-sound pairs; this is the one that finds a changed surname. deduping measured the current routes catching only 42.9% of 37,467 verified surname-change pairs, and this lifting it to 67.2%.
blocking_rules.sql: l.forename_metaphone = r.forename_metaphone AND l.dob_year_clean = r.dob_year_clean AND l.dob_month_clean = r.dob_month_clean AND l.surname_metaphone <> r.surname_metaphone

blocking_rules.description: deduping route 6, the no-date rescue: both name sounds agree and at least one side has no usable birth year, so route 1 could never have seen the pair.
blocking_rules.sql: l.surname_metaphone = r.surname_metaphone AND l.forename_metaphone = r.forename_metaphone AND (l.dob_year_clean IS NULL OR r.dob_year_clean IS NULL)

comparisons.description: Surname, term frequency on: agreeing on FOTHERGILL is far stronger evidence than agreeing on SMITH.
Forename after the nickname lookup, so ROBERT and BOB have already met.
Middle names. Most filings carry none, so most pairs land on the null level and are neither helped nor punished.
Birth year, exact. No term-frequency adjustment: a birth year is not a name, and down-weighting a common year is what let a 37-year gap score 1.0 in the first sample run.
Birth month, exact. Compared separately from the year so that agreeing on both is two pieces of evidence and disagreeing on either costs something.
Nationality, home nations collapsed. Term frequency on, because agreeing on LATVIAN says more than agreeing on BRITISH.
Postcode at full, sector, district and area level. Formation-agent postcodes are already nulled by the cleaning, which is what makes this safe to score on at all.

person._lost_in_translation: deduping used three custom comparison ladders this settings document cannot express, and the nuance moves to the model features instead. (1) dob_joint: one comparison over year AND month with a graded 'year off by one, same month' level. Here the year is an exact comparison and the month is carried by the blocking, and dob_year_gap / dob_month_equal are features. (2) address_freq: postcode levels split by how many records share that postcode (rare <=20, mid <=1000, then district). cl.PostcodeComparison has the geographic ladder but not the frequency split; the junk-postcode nullify removes the worst of it and the model sees postcode_equal and postcode_district_equal. (3) Every comparison there ended in a fixed neutral else with the EM output clamped so no interior level could become a penalty; this document has no clamp, so a level CAN learn a penalty here.
person._em_note: Two rules on purpose. Splink cannot estimate a comparison whose columns the training rule holds equal, so one rule fixes the name sounds (and estimates the date of birth, nationality and postcode) and the other fixes the date of birth (and estimates the names). With the single name+DOB rule this file shipped with, dob_year_clean came back m=None on every level: the comparison was dead weight, and pairs 37 birth-years apart scored 1.0.

blocking_rules.description: Same core name. deduping's first corporate route.
Same core-name sound and the same kind of body, so a GmbH and a trust of similar name are not compared.
Same registration number, whatever the name says.
Same first word of the core name and the same postcode district: a renamed company at one address.

comparisons.description: The name with the legal form split off. The main signal on this track.
Sorted distinct words of the core name, on overlap. Catches a different word order and a dropped word.
Registration number. Strong when present; the exact keys have usually taken these already.
Country of registration as a short code.
What kind of body it is. Weak alone; it mainly keeps a trust apart from a company of the same name.
Postcode at full, sector, district and area level.

organisation._em_note: Two rules, so no comparison is held equal by all of them. With only the name+type rule, type_bucket never varied inside the training block and came back untrained — the same silent failure the person track had.

_budget_note: max_pairs is sized for the 500,000-record development sample, where the person routes cost a few million pairs. deduping measured its six routes at 19.2M / 7.3M / 3.2M / 0.18M pairs over 5.16 MILLION representatives, so the full 16-million-record snapshot will need this raised to roughly 60,000,000 for the person track, and the blocking cost check (D17) has to pass before Splink starts. The budget is deliberately left at the sample's scale so a full run fails loudly rather than quietly taking the machine.
